title: Dispersion
outcomes: Explain why averages need a measure of spread and distinguish absolute from relative measures of dispersion.
Compute range, mean deviation, standard deviation, variance and quartile deviation, with their coefficients, for raw and grouped data.
Use the coefficient of variation to compare consistency of two or more series.
Apply the properties — effect of change of origin and scale, SD of a constant, combined SD, corrected SD, SD of the first n natural numbers and of two numbers.
Choose the right measure (e.g. QD for open-end classes) and avoid the common traps.

meta.exam_tip: Dispersion MCQs are formula-driven and quick: change of origin/scale, CV comparisons, combined SD, SD of two numbers and of first n natural numbers. Remember ICAI expresses coefficients as percentages (× 100).

concepts.title: Why dispersion? Absolute vs relative measures
body: Two series can have the same average and yet look nothing alike: 50, 50, 50 and 0, 50, 100 both average 50. Dispersion measures how far observations are scattered around their central value.

Absolute measures — range, mean deviation (MD), standard deviation (SD) and quartile deviation (QD) — are in the unit of the data. Relative measures — coefficient of range, coefficient of MD, coefficient of variation (CV) and coefficient of QD — are unit-free.
To compare two or more distributions (different units or very different averages) use relative measures. Relative measures are a little harder to compute and understand than absolute ones.
concepts.analogy: Average height tells you how tall a class is; dispersion tells you whether the class photo needs a step-stool row.
concepts.work: Two branches with the same average debtor days but very different spreads need different credit controls. Investors look at volatility (SD of returns), not only average return.

concepts.title: Range and coefficient of range
body: Range = L − S (largest − smallest). Coefficient of range = (L − S)/(L + S) × 100.
For grouped data, range = upper boundary of the last class − lower boundary of the first class; the coefficient uses the same two boundaries.
Range is unaffected by a change of origin but changes by |b| under a change of scale: if y = a + bx, R(y) = |b| × R(x).
Simple and quick (useful in quality control and price movements), but based only on two extreme values, so it is not an ideal measure.
concepts.analogy: Range is judging a road trip only by its highest and lowest altitude — ignoring everything in between.
concepts.work: A stock's 52-week high–low range is printed in every market report; quality control charts use the range of small samples.

concepts.title: Mean deviation
body: Mean deviation is the arithmetic mean of absolute deviations from a central value A (mean, median or mode): MD = Σ|x − A|/n; grouped: Σf|x − A|/N.
Coefficient of MD = MD about A ÷ A × 100.
MD is minimum when deviations are taken from the median. It is unaffected by a change of origin and changes in the same ratio as a change of scale: MD(y) = |b| × MD(x).
It uses all observations, but ignoring signs makes it awkward for further algebra.
concepts.analogy: MD is the average distance each house in a lane is from the lane's centre — direction does not matter.
concepts.work: Forecast accuracy is often reported as mean absolute deviation (MAD) of actual from budgeted sales.

concepts.title: Standard deviation, variance and coefficient of variation
body: SD (σ or s) is the root-mean-square deviation from the AM: s = √(Σ(x − x̄)²/n) = √(Σx²/n − x̄²). Variance = s². Grouped: s = √(Σfd²/N − (Σfd/N)²) × C with d = (x − A)/C.
CV = s/x̄ × 100. The series with the lower CV is more consistent (stable, uniform); the higher CV is more variable.

Properties: (i) if all values are equal, SD = 0 (true also for range and MD); (ii) SD is unaffected by change of origin and affected by change of scale: if y = a + bx, s(y) = |b| s(x) and variance(y) = b² variance(x); (iii) combined SD of two groups: s = √[(n₁s₁² + n₂s₂² + n₁d₁² + n₂d₂²)/(n₁ + n₂)] with dᵢ = x̄ᵢ − x̄ (combined mean). Extends to k groups; if the means are equal, d terms vanish.
Useful results: SD of the first n natural numbers = √((n² − 1)/12); SD of two numbers a and b = |a − b|/2. A wrong observation is corrected by fixing Σx and Σx² and recomputing.
SD is the best measure of dispersion — rigidly defined, based on all values and suited to algebraic treatment — though more affected by extreme values than QD.
concepts.analogy: SD is the "typical miss" of an archer around the bull's-eye; CV is that miss relative to the size of the target.
concepts.work: Portfolio risk, process capability in cost audits and sampling precision in audit all rest on SD. CV is how you compare the stability of a ₹10 crore branch with a ₹500 crore one.

concepts.title: Quartile deviation and choosing a measure
body: QD (semi-interquartile range) = (Q₃ − Q₁)/2. Coefficient of QD = (Q₃ − Q₁)/(Q₃ + Q₁) × 100.

QD is the best measure for open-end classes and is less affected by extreme values and sampling fluctuations, because it uses only the middle 50% of the data. Like the others, it is unaffected by change of origin and changes by |b| with change of scale.
Choice: SD for general use and further analysis; CV for comparing consistency; QD for open-end or highly skewed data; range for a quick look.
concepts.analogy: QD ignores the two noisiest quarters of a crowd and measures how spread the calm middle half is.
concepts.work: Salary surveys report the interquartile band (Q₁–Q₃) because a few very high or very low pay packets would distort SD.

illustrations.title: Range and quartile deviation
illustrations.q: (a) Closing prices (₹) of a share for 7 days: 412, 398, 431, 405, 420, 389, 427. Find the range and its coefficient. (b) For inclusive classes 10–19 to 50–59, find range and coefficient. (c) For the data 22, 27, 31, 35, 38, 41, 45, 52, 58, 66, find QD and its coefficient.

checks.label: range of grouped data from extreme boundaries

illustrations.title: Mean deviation about mean and about median
illustrations.q: For 5, 8, 10, 13, 20, 28 find the mean deviation about the mean and about the median, and their coefficients.

solution.title: Result
solution.text: MD about mean = 40/6 = 6.67 (coefficient 47.62); MD about median = 38/6 = 6.33 (coefficient 55.07). MD about the median is smaller — as the minimum property says.

illustrations.title: SD and CV of a grouped distribution; comparing consistency
illustrations.q: (a) Weekly sales of 50 outlets: 0–10: 4, 10–20: 10, 20–30: 16, 30–40: 12, 40–50: 8. Find mean, SD and CV. (b) Batsman A averages 48 runs with SD 12; batsman B averages 36 with SD 7.2. Who is more consistent?

solution.title: (b)
solution.text: CV(A) = 12/48 × 100 = 25%; CV(B) = 7.2/36 × 100 = 20%. B is more consistent (lower CV), although A scores more on average.

illustrations.title: Combined SD, corrected SD and two handy results
illustrations.q: (a) Group 1: n = 40, mean 50, SD 6. Group 2: n = 60, mean 60, SD 8. Find the combined SD. (b) 20 observations have mean 40 and SD 5; one value 53 was wrongly recorded for 35. Correct the mean and SD. (c) SD of 1, 2, …, 10? (d) SD of 8 and 20?

jobs.title: Comparing branch performance fairly
jobs.role: Internal auditor of a cooperative bank
jobs.situation: Branch X (large) has average monthly deposits growth of ₹40 lakh with SD ₹12 lakh; branch Y (small) ₹8 lakh with SD ₹4 lakh. The board asks which is "more erratic".
steps: SDs are in the same unit but the branches differ hugely in size, so compare CVs, not SDs.
Branch Y is more erratic relative to its size, though its SD is smaller.
Investigate Y's volatility — concentration on a few large depositors is a typical cause.
jobs.takeaway: Absolute spread can mislead when scales differ; CV makes the comparison fair.

jobs.title: Fixing a statistic after a data-entry error
jobs.role: Analyst in a corporate FP&A team
jobs.situation: A dashboard shows mean and SD of 250 daily dispatch quantities. You find one day keyed as 9,800 instead of 980.
steps: Do not recompute from scratch if raw data are not handy — use Σx = n x̄ and Σx² = n(s² + x̄²).
Subtract the wrong value (and its square), add the right one, then recompute mean and SD.
Document the correction and the source document, as the auditor will ask for it.
jobs.takeaway: Means and SDs can be corrected from totals alone — keep Σx and Σx² in your working papers.

mcqs.explain: Range depends only on the two extremes.

questions.q: Daily output of 50 machines: 100–120: 6, 120–140: 14, 140–160: 20, 160–180: 10. Compute the mean, standard deviation and coefficient of variation.

scheme.pt: d, fd, fd² columns and totals

remarks: The most common slip is forgetting to multiply by the class width C.
Some candidates divide Σfd² by N but forget to subtract (Σfd/N)².
tips: Keep d small (−2, −1, 0, 1) to avoid arithmetic errors.

questions.q: Factory A employs 50 workers with mean monthly bonus ₹4,500 and SD ₹300. Factory B employs 70 workers with mean ₹5,100 and SD ₹400. Find the combined mean and combined SD.
remarks: Leaving out the n·d² terms understates the combined SD.
mistakes: Using SD instead of variance inside the formula.
tips: Write the formula first; examiners give a step mark for it.

questions.q: For the ordered data 14, 19, 23, 26, 30, 34, 37, 45, 51: (a) find the quartile deviation and its coefficient; (b) find the mean deviation about the median and its coefficient.
remarks: Many write the interquartile range (20) as QD.
tips: Show the positions (2.5th, 7.5th) before the values.

summary: Absolute (range, MD, SD, QD) vs relative (coefficients, CV) measures.
Range = L − S; coefficient (L − S)/(L + S) × 100.
MD = Σ|x − A|/n; minimum about the median.
SD = √(Σx²/n − x̄²); CV = s/x̄ × 100; lower CV = more consistent.
QD = (Q₃ − Q₁)/2; best for open-end classes.
All are unaffected by change of origin and multiplied by |b| under change of scale.
remember: SD of first n natural numbers = √((n² − 1)/12).
traps: Dispersion measures are never negative — take |b|.
Grouped range uses boundaries, not limits.
A higher mean does not mean more consistent — compare CVs.
Interquartile range is Q₃ − Q₁; QD is half of it.

viva.q: What is the difference between absolute and relative measures of dispersion?
viva.model: Absolute measures such as range, mean deviation, standard deviation and quartile deviation are expressed in the unit of the data, so they cannot compare series in different units or with very different averages. Relative measures, the coefficients such as the coefficient of variation, are ratios or percentages and are unit-free, so they are used for comparing two or more distributions; but they are a little harder to compute.

viva.q: State the properties of standard deviation.
viva.model: If all observations are equal, the standard deviation is zero. It is not affected by a change of origin but is affected by a change of scale: if y equals a plus b x, the SD of y is the absolute value of b times the SD of x. And the SD of two groups can be combined using their sizes, means and SDs.

viva.q: What is the coefficient of variation and how is it used to compare consistency?
viva.model: The coefficient of variation is the standard deviation divided by the mean, multiplied by one hundred. It is a relative, unit-free measure. When comparing two series, the one with the lower coefficient of variation is more consistent or more stable, and the one with the higher CV is more variable.

viva.q: What is quartile deviation, and when is it the most suitable measure of dispersion?
viva.model: Quartile deviation, or the semi-interquartile range, is half the difference between the third and the first quartile, that is Q3 minus Q1 divided by two. Its coefficient is Q3 minus Q1 over Q3 plus Q1, times one hundred. It is the best measure for open-end classifications and is less affected by extreme values, because it ignores the lowest and highest quarters of the data.

viva.q: What are the merits and demerits of range as a measure of dispersion?
viva.model: Range is the difference between the largest and smallest observations. It is very simple to understand and to calculate, and it is used in quality control and for stock price movements. But it depends only on the two extreme values, so it ignores all other observations, is greatly affected by extremes, and cannot be found for open-end classes. So it is not an ideal measure.

viva.q: About which value is the mean deviation minimum, and how does it behave under change of origin and scale?
viva.model: Mean deviation is minimum when the deviations are taken about the median. Like other measures of dispersion, it does not change with a change of origin, but it changes in the same ratio as a change of scale: the mean deviation of y is the absolute value of b times that of x when y equals a plus b x.

cases.title: Choosing the steadier of two mutual funds
cases.case: A client asks her CA which of two equity funds has been steadier. Over the last 36 months, Fund A gave a mean monthly return of 1.4% with a standard deviation of 4.2%; Fund B gave a mean of 1.2% with a standard deviation of 3.0%. Fund A's best and worst months were +11.5% and −9.1%. The client also asks what would happen to the figures if a flat 0.1% monthly fee were deducted from every return.

mcqs.q: What is the coefficient of variation of Fund A?
Which fund is more consistent, and why?
options: Fund B — its CV (250%) is lower
Fund A — its mean is higher
Fund A — its CV is higher
mcqs.explain: Consistency is judged by the relative measure; lower CV means more consistent. Fund B: 3.0/1.2 × 100 = 250% < 300%.

mcqs.q: What is the range of Fund A's monthly returns?
mcqs.explain: Range = largest − smallest = 11.5 − (−9.1) = 20.6 percentage points.

mcqs.q: If a flat 0.1% fee is deducted from every monthly return, Fund A's standard deviation will:
options: Depend on the number of months
mcqs.explain: Subtracting a constant is a change of origin; SD is unaffected by change of origin (the mean falls to 1.3%, so CV does change).
